# Introduction

Speed and agility tests are a standard part of the monitoring of young athletes.
To time them accurately, timing gates (photoelectric cells) are usually used.
This equipment is expensive: about €1,500 to €3,000 for a kit of a few gates
(Microgate Witty, Tendo Sprint System). It also takes time to set up and to
learn how to use. For many sports structures, spending such an amount for a
few tests per year is not realistic, especially since the monitoring of young
players does not require a precision to the thousandth of a second.

The most common alternative, the hand-held stopwatch, is not satisfactory
either: the coach's reaction time at the start and at the finish introduces an
error, whereas on a test lasting about fifteen seconds, a few tenths of a second
can change the interpretation.

The My Jump app (Balsalobre-Fernández et al., 2015) showed that a smartphone
filming in slow motion can accurately measure a performance by manually
selecting key frames. We applied the same principle: the test is filmed in slow
motion (240 frames per second), the user selects the start frame and the finish
frame, and the program computes the time.

This project addresses two questions:

1. Can we build a simple, low-cost video tool to time any test that starts and
   finishes on the same line?
2. Applied to the Illinois agility test, can this tool highlight a relationship
   between time and age in young ice hockey players?
   
# Data

**Participants.** Twenty young ice hockey players (17 boys, 3 girls), aged
8.8 to 17.7 years, performed the Illinois agility test during the 2026 autumn
holiday camp.

**Test conditions.** The test was performed off-ice, on a concrete car park.
It had rained the day before, so the ground was still damp and rather slippery.
Before the test, players coming from an on-ice session did a brief warm-up;
the others did a full warm-up (running drills, slaloms and sprints).

**Protocol.** Players started standing, 1 m behind the start/finish line.
Each player performed one trial; players aged U13 and under could perform a
second trial if they wished, and the best of the two was kept. On the video,
the start frame and the finish frame are the frames where the player's hips
are level with the cone marking the start/finish line. The test time is
therefore the time between the two crossings of this line by the hips.

**Video acquisition.** Videos were recorded with an iPhone 13 in slow-motion
mode (240 frames per second), fixed on a tripod 2–3 m from the start cone,
facing the start/finish line. A single camera is enough, since the start and
the finish are on the same line.

**Privacy.** As the participants are minors, videos, names and birth dates are
not shared. Each player is given an anonymous id (P01 to P20). Only the age at
the time of the test and the sex are published, in the file
`results/measures_anonymous.csv`.

# Methods: Python (video timing tool)

## General workflow

For each video, the user gives the real recording frequency; a window then
shows the video frame by frame. The user moves with the arrow keys or a
progress bar, presses Enter on the start frame, then on the finish frame.
The time is computed as:

$$\text{time} = \frac{\text{finish frame} - \text{start frame}}{\text{recording frequency}}$$

The result is saved in a CSV file after each video.

## The recording frequency trap

In slow-motion mode, the iPhone records at 240 frames per second but stores
the video so that it is played at 30 frames per second: this is what creates
the slow-motion effect. The video file therefore states 30 frames/s, a wrong
value for our computation.

Example with one of our videos, which contains 5,522 frames:

- with the frequency stored in the file: 5,522 / 30 = 184 s, i.e. more than
  3 minutes, which is impossible;
- with the real frequency: 5,522 / 240 = 23 s, which matches the real
  duration of the video.

The error is a factor of 8 (240 / 30). The same applies to the test time:
a player whose start frame is 646 and finish frame is 5,217 has a time of
4,571 / 240 = 19.05 s. With the frequency of the file, we would have obtained
4,571 / 30 = 152.4 s.

The program therefore does not rely on the frequency stored in the file:
it displays it for information, then **asks the user for the real frequency**
(240 by default).

The frequency also sets the precision of the measurement. At 240 frames/s,
one frame lasts 1/240 = 4.2 ms; at 30 frames/s, it would last 33 ms.
Slow motion makes the measurement 8 times more precise.

## Anonymisation and data protection

The participants are minors. Their name, birth date and image are personal
data that must not appear in a public GitHub repository: the image-rights
authorisation signed for the camp covers use by the structure, not public
distribution on the Internet. The videos are also too large (about 200 MB
each) for GitHub, which is limited to 100 MB per file.

This was solved as follows:

- each player receives an **anonymous id** (P01 to P20), assigned
  automatically by the program;
- the **birth date** is only used to compute the **age at the time of the
  test**; only this age is published;
- the files containing personal information (videos, measures with names,
  name → id correspondence table, birth dates) **stay only on my computer**;
  the `.gitignore` file prevents them from being sent to GitHub;
- the only published results file, `results/measures_anonymous.csv`,
  contains only the id, the frame numbers, the frequency, the time, the age
  and the sex.

Thanks to the `MEASURE = False` switch in `main.ipynb`, the project runs
without the videos: it directly reads this anonymous file.

## Code organisation

The Python code is split into two files:

- `main.ipynb` is the **entry point**: it only contains the settings
  (folders, `MEASURE` switch) and the function calls;
- `sources/video_timing.py` contains **all the functions**, grouped by theme:
  video information, display, measurement, results files, anonymisation.

The notebook thus stays short and readable, and each function can be modified
without affecting the rest.

| Theme | Function | Input | Output | Role |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Video information** | `get_video_info` | video path | file frequency, number of frames | read the video information |
| | `ask_fps` | file frequency, default frequency (240) | real frequency | ask the user for the real frequency, rejecting invalid values |
| | `get_name_from_file` | video path | player name | read the player's name from the file name (spaces become `_`) |
| **Display** | `put_text` | image, text, position, colour, size | (modified image) | write a text with a black outline, readable on any background |
| | `frame_to_x` | frame number, number of frames, width | horizontal position | convert a frame number into a position on the progress bar |
| | `draw_display` | frame, position, number of frames, frequency, start, finish | image to display | assemble the frame, the texts (time, START/END) and the progress bar |
| **Measurement** | `measure_test` | video path, real frequency, display scale | name, start and finish frames, frequency, time (or nothing if cancelled) | open the measurement window, handle the keyboard, compute the time |
| | `on_mouse` (inside `measure_test`) | mouse event, position | (updated position) | jump in the video by clicking or dragging on the bar |
| **Results files** | `list_videos` | folder | sorted list of videos | find the video files in the folder (.mov, .mp4, .m4v, .avi) |
| | `load_results` | CSV file | results table | read the results, or return an empty table if the file does not exist |
| | `save_result` | result, CSV file | (updated file) | save a result, replacing the old one if the video was already measured |
| | `measure_all_videos` | folder, CSV file, frequency, `redo` option | (updated file) | measure all videos one after the other, skipping those already done |
| **Anonymisation** | `make_id_table` | list of names, correspondence file | name → id table | assign the ids P01, P02…, never changing those already given |
| | `anonymize_results` | measures, id table, dates, output file | anonymous file | create the published file: id, frames, frequency, time, age, sex |

## A privacy error corrected with Git

During the first upload to GitHub, the file `data/children_info.csv`, which
contains the names and birth dates, was published by mistake: the line that
should have excluded it had been forgotten in the `.gitignore`. The repository
was still private, so the file was never publicly visible. The error was
spotted by checking the list of uploaded files.

Simply deleting the file would not have been enough: it would have remained
visible in the Git history. The correction was done in four steps:

1. add `data/children_info.csv` to the `.gitignore`;
2. `git rm --cached data/children_info.csv`: remove the file from Git without
   deleting it from the computer;
3. `git commit --amend`: replace the first commit with a version without
   this file;
4. `git push --force`: replace the version stored on GitHub.

As GitHub can keep an old commit accessible through a direct link, the
repository was deleted and published again before being made public.
Lesson learned: always check the list of uploaded files before the first commit.

# Results

## Ranking of the players

```{r}
#| label: fig-ranking
#| fig-cap: "Illinois time of each player, from the fastest (top) to the slowest (bottom). Black line: median; blue dashed: Q1; red dashed: Q3."

data_rank <- data[order(data$time_video), ]
data_rank$group <- "Other"
data_rank$group[1] <- "Fastest"
data_rank$group[nrow(data_rank)] <- "Slowest"
data_rank$id <- factor(data_rank$id, levels = rev(data_rank$id))
q <- quantile(data_rank$time_video, probs = c(0.25, 0.50, 0.75))

ggplot(data_rank, aes(x = time_video, y = id, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = q[1], colour = "blue",  linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = q[2], colour = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = q[3], colour = "red",   linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f s", time_video)), hjust = -0.1, size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Fastest = "forestgreen", Slowest = "orange", Other = "grey70")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, max(data_rank$time_video) * 1.12)) +
  labs(x = "Time (s)", y = "Player", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "top")
```

<!-- 2-3 sentences: median, Q1, Q3, fastest and slowest times. -->

## Time and age

```{r}
#| label: fig-age
#| fig-cap: "Illinois time according to age. Line: linear regression and its 95% confidence interval."

ggplot(data, aes(x = age_years, y = time_video)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, colour = "black", fill = "grey80") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = sex), size = 3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(F = "tomato", M = "steelblue")) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Illinois time (s)", colour = "Sex") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-regression
#| tbl-cap: "Linear regression of the Illinois time on age."

model <- lm(time_video ~ age_years, data = data)
knitr::kable(summary(model)$coefficients, digits = 4,
             col.names = c("Estimate", "Std. error", "t", "p"))
```

<!-- Report: r = -0.73 (95% CI -0.89 to -0.43, p < 0.001),
     slope = -0.42 s per year, R² = 0.54, residuals normal (Shapiro p = 0.44). -->
